title: Hannah's quiet prayer (1 Samuel 1:13)
hookLine: Hannah's lips moved but her voice wasn't heard; the rabbis made her the model of the silent Amidah

cards: Shiloh, in the days of the judges. The sanctuary is busy with families who've come for the yearly offering. One woman isn't eating.

Hannah has no children, and her husband's other wife, who has several, has been needling her about it for years. She gets up, goes to the sanctuary, and prays. The old priest Eli sits by the doorpost, watching.
Her lips are moving. No sound comes out. He comes to a conclusion, and it's the wrong one.

teach.b: First Samuel tells it in one verse. In the old Jewish translation: Hannah "spoke in her heart; only her lips moved," but her voice couldn't be heard, and Eli thought she was drunk. He scolds her: put away your wine.

She answers with great dignity: I'm not drunk, I'm a woman in deep sorrow, pouring out my soul before the Lord. Eli changes his tune and blesses her. In time she has a son, Samuel, who grows up to be a prophet.
The rabbis read this scene very closely. In Berakhot 31a, the Talmud says: how many great laws can be learned from Hannah's prayer. She spoke in her heart: so the one who prays must direct the heart.
Only her lips moved: so you form the words with your lips, not only in your head. Her voice couldn't be heard: so the Amidah is said quietly, not shouted.
And Eli thought she was drunk: so a drunk person shouldn't pray.

teach.h: THE WHOLE ROOM PRAYS LIKE HANNAH.
teach.b: Look who this makes the teacher. Not a priest, not a king, not a prophet. A woman the priest misjudged, praying in tears, about something everyone around her had stopped asking about.
To this day, when a whole synagogue stands in near silence with lips moving, they're praying the way Hannah prayed at Shiloh.

how: Jews say the Amidah in a whisper, forming the words with the lips so they can hear themselves but the person beside them can't; the Talmud draws these rules from Hannah's prayer at Shiloh.

o: the matriarch who laughed at the promise of a son
the prophet who anointed Israel's first king
the woman at Shiloh whose lips moved in prayer

games.q: laws from Hannah — tap the pairs.
p: form the words with your lips

s: Eli recognized at once that Hannah was praying
he thought she was drunk, and only blessed her after she explained.
the Talmud learns several laws of prayer from Hannah
Berakhot 31a draws laws of the Amidah from her verse.
the Amidah is meant to be shouted with feeling
like Hannah, it's said with moving lips and a voice others can't hear.

games.q: you're Hannah. the priest has just accused you of being drunk in the sanctuary. what do you do?
o: explain, with dignity, that you're pouring out your soul.
argue that he has no right to judge you.
games.why: she tells him she's a woman in sorrow, pouring out her soul. Eli blesses her, and in time Samuel is born.

practice: Think of something heavy for you, the kind of thing you've stopped mentioning to anyone, and say a sentence or two about it with your lips moving but no sound.
If you pray, speak it to God, the way Hannah did; if not, speak it to the quiet. Your mouth is part of it now.

wordCard.voice: Hannah. The woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without a sound — the rabbis' model for how the Amidah, prayer of the heart, is said.

orig.note: Hebrew: speaking on her heart. 1 Samuel 1:13, the root of praying from the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: hannah prayed quietly. The model for the Amidah is a private prayer, once mistaken for drunkenness. Day five hundred seventy-six, done.

sources.q: spoke in her heart; only her lips moved
